messages.content:
You review lifestyle plans written by FOXO's lifestyle coach for a member in India.

You will see the member's profile, the abnormal results the plan targets, and the full plan. Judge whether a member could act on the plan tomorrow. Do not judge medical correctness here; other checks cover that.

For each criterion, first write one or two sentences of reasoning, then set passed to true or false.

Criteria (use these ids exactly, one entry each):
- specific: Recommendations give concrete foods with portions or timing, not generic advice like "eat healthy".
- practical: The foods are everyday Indian foods a member could easily buy and cook.
- explained: Each recommendation says how it helps the linked biomarker.
- activity_concrete: The activity advice says what to do, for how long and how often.

Respond with a single JSON object that matches this JSON schema:
{"$defs": {"CriterionVerdict": {"properties": {"criterion": {"title": "Criterion", "type": "string"}, "reasoning": {"title": "Reasoning", "type": "string"}, "passed": {"title": "Passed", "type": "boolean"}}, "required": ["criterion", "reasoning", "passed"], "title": "CriterionVerdict", "type": "object"}}, "properties": {"criteria": {"items": {"$ref": "#/$defs/CriterionVerdict"}, "title": "Criteria", "type": "array"}}, "required": ["criteria"], "title": "JudgeOutput", "type": "object"}

Diet: vegan. Allergies: none. Conditions: none.
Abnormal results: vitamin_b12 160.0 pg/mL (low), haemoglobin 11.2 g/dL (low)

Plan:
Focus areas: vitamin_b12; haemoglobin; plant-based iron absorption; energy levels and fatigue
Foods to eat:
- B12-fortified plant milk (soy or almond): 200 ml with breakfast and 200 ml as an evening drink, both from a carton that says 'fortified with vitamin B12'. (why: Plant foods are naturally almost free of B12, so fortified plant milks are the main reliable vegan source. Two 200 ml servings daily give a steady intake through the day rather than one large dose.; linked to vitamin_b12)
- B12-fortified breakfast cereal or fortified oats: 4-5 tablespoons (about 40 g) with the fortified plant milk, 4-5 mornings a week. Check the label for 'fortified with vitamin B12'. (why: Fortified cereals are a second everyday vegan B12 source, so you are not dependent on a single food. Choosing them at breakfast also sets up a regular daily habit.; linked to vitamin_b12)
- Sprouted moong or chana: 1 small bowl (about 100 g) at lunch or as a mid-morning snack, always squeezed with lemon or eaten with a few slices of amla, guava or orange. (why: Sprouting lowers phytates so more of the iron is absorbed, and the vitamin C from lemon/amla/guava converts plant iron into a form the body takes up far better. This is a practical vegan way to lift haemoglobin.; linked to haemoglobin)
- One iron-rich dal or legume at both lunch and dinner: 1 katori (about 150 g cooked) of masoor, chana, rajma, moth beans or black-eyed peas. Pair each meal with lemon squeezed on top or a small piece of amla/guava after eating. (why: Pulses are the backbone of vegan iron intake. Eating them at two meals plus a vitamin C source at the same meal improves absorption and supports red blood cell production.; linked to haemoglobin)
- Ragi or bajra instead of white rice at dinner: 2 ragi rotis or 1 bajra roti with sabzi, at least 5 nights a week. (why: Millets carry noticeably more iron and folate than polished rice, and swapping them in is an easy, low-cost change that adds to your daily iron load.; linked to haemoglobin)
- Dark green leafy sabzi (palak, methi, amaranth/chauli, drumstick leaves): 1 katori cooked at lunch 4-5 times a week, lightly cooked and served with lemon. (why: Leafy greens supply both iron and folate, and folate is needed alongside B12 to build healthy red blood cells. Light cooking plus lemon keeps the folate and improves iron uptake.; linked to haemoglobin)
- Til (sesame) chutney or roasted sesame powder: 1 tablespoon daily sprinkled on dal, rice or roti. (why: Sesame is one of the richest vegan iron foods in Indian kitchens and is easy to add in small daily amounts without changing your whole menu.; linked to haemoglobin)
- Keep a 2-hour gap: tea or coffee only between meals, never with or just after a meal. Have lemon water, nimbu pani without sugar, or plain water with meals instead. (why: Tea and coffee tannins block iron absorption from plant foods when taken with meals. Simply shifting the timing can meaningfully raise the iron you actually absorb.; linked to haemoglobin)
- Soak dals and whole legumes for 6-8 hours and discard the water before cooking; sprout where possible. (why: Soaking and sprouting reduce phytates that bind iron, so the same dal delivers more usable iron without needing more food.; linked to haemoglobin)
- Ask your FOXO doctor whether a vitamin B12 supplement is needed for you, since fortified foods alone may not be enough at your level. (why: With B12 at 160 pg/mL, food sources help but a clinician should decide if supplementation is required, and at what dose. FOXO's doctor will advise on this.; linked to vitamin_b12)
Foods to limit or avoid: Tea and coffee within 1 hour before or after meals (keep a 2-hour gap); Polished white rice and maida replacing millets at most meals; Deep-fried snacks, pakoras and bakery items as daily staples; Sugary drinks, packaged fruit juices and sweetened health drinks; Alcohol, which reduces B12 and folate absorption; Very high-fibre bran-heavy meals taken at the same time as iron-rich foods, as they reduce iron absorption; Calcium-fortified drinks or calcium-rich foods taken together with your main iron meal (keep a gap of 2 hours); Long, unsoaked cooking of whole legumes as the only dal option
Activity: No exercise restriction has been advised by your doctor. Start with a brisk 30-minute walk 5 days a week, and add gentle bodyweight strength work 2 days a week (10-15 squats, wall push-ups, band rows). Add 10 minutes of stretching or simple yoga daily. Because your haemoglobin is low, if you feel dizzy, breathless or unusually tired during activity, stop and rest, keep the session light, and follow your doctor's advice.
Sleep: Aim for 7-8 hours of sleep with a fixed bedtime and wake time, screens off 45 minutes before bed, and the room dark and cool. Short 15-20 minute rest breaks in the afternoon are fine if fatigue from low haemoglobin builds up.
Retest in 12 weeks

Nothing is left as generic 'eat healthy' advice.", "passed": true}, {"criterion": "practical", "reasoning": "The foods are standard Indian kitchen items: moong/chana sprouts, masoor/rajma dals, ragi and bajra rotis, palak/methi sabzi, til chutney, lemon, amla and guava. Fortified plant milk and fortified cereal require label-checking but are widely available in Indian stores, so a member could buy and cook all of this easily.", "passed": true}, {"criterion": "explained", "reasoning": "Each item carries a 'why' clause tied to its biomarker: fortified milks/cereals explained as reliable vegan B12 sources, sprouting and vitamin C pairing explained as improving plant iron uptake for haemoglobin, millets and greens explained as iron/folate sources, and tea timing explained via tannin blocking of iron absorption.
